lead: A layout is only useful if the fab can actually print it. Design rules are the minimum widths, spacings, overlaps and enclosures that a drawn shape must obey so that every mask prints, aligns and etches without breaks or shorts. Foundries publish these rules as a contract; designers draw to them, and a computer program checks every shape before the file is sent out. The same rules shape every standard cell, every SRAM bitcell and every pad ring in a chip.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for which layers exist, and Chapter 2.2 for why alignment errors happen.

sections.h3: Why a drawn shape needs a rule

blocks.text: A layout is a stack of rectangles, one set per layer. Each layer becomes a mask, and the fab prints that mask onto the wafer. Three things go wrong during printing.

items: Mask misalignment: the next mask lands a little off the one below. A contact drawn exactly on the metal edge may end up half outside it.
Etch bias: the etch cuts sideways as well as down, so each edge of a shape can move outward or inward by a small amount; a line or gap can print narrower or wider than drawn.
Finite resolution: the printer cannot form features below some size. Corners round off and very thin lines simply disappear.

blocks.text: A rule is a margin bought against these errors. Two shapes on the same mask move together, so mask misalignment does not change their spacing. The spacing rule guards against variation in printed size: if random variation lets each edge of a shape move outward by as much as δ (resist and etch bias, or lithographic variation), a gap shrinks by 2δ, so minimum spacing must exceed 2δ. Misalignment Δ enters only the rules between different layers, which is why overlap and enclosure must exceed Δ. Rules are therefore not laws of physics; they are a contract between the designer and the foundry.
A layout that breaks a rule is rejected before fabrication. A layout that obeys every rule still has to work electrically, which is a separate question.

Writing every rule in micrometres makes the rule set useless the moment the process shrinks. Instead, most teaching rule sets use one length unit, λ (lambda), chosen by the foundry. All rules are then whole multiples of λ.

blocks.where: L is the drawn length in micrometres, n is the rule expressed in λ (a pure number), and λ is the unit length in micrometres, often half the smallest drawn feature.

blocks.text: A layout drawn in λ can be moved to a new process by changing one number. Some syllabi call these scalable design rules. Production processes instead publish micron rules, absolute values in μm or nm, which are tighter and layer-specific.

λ is not the wavelength of the lithography light. The wavelength is a property of the printer and is written in nm; λ here is only a drawing unit. Mixing the two is the commonest slip in an exam answer.
Every rule set, however large, is built from a few families.

items: Minimum width: the narrowest rectangle allowed on a layer. A thinner line may break during etch.
Minimum spacing: the smallest gap allowed between two shapes on the same layer. A smaller gap may short.
Minimum overlap: two layers that must connect need at least this much shared area, so a misalignment still leaves contact.
Enclosure: one layer must surround another on all sides, for example metal around a contact.
Extension: one layer must stick out past another by a set amount, for example poly past the diffusion at the gate edge.
Separation between unrelated layers: a minimum distance between layers that never connect, to limit coupling and etch interference.

blocks.text: Minimum pitch is not a separate rule; it follows from the other two. For wires on one layer, pitch equals minimum width plus minimum spacing, measured centre to centre.

sections.h3: Checking the rules, and wire resistance

blocks.text: A design rule checker (DRC) reads the layout file, rebuilds each layer from the drawn shapes, and tests every rule on every pair of shapes. Real decks run to hundreds or thousands of rules. One violation blocks the design. DRC is only one check; a layout-versus-schematic (LVS) check confirms the drawn circuit matches the intended netlist, and parasitic extraction follows.
Rules also decide how much resistance a wire adds. A wire of uniform width is counted in squares, and each square contributes the same resistance however large the square is.

blocks.where: R is the wire resistance in Ω, R_s is the sheet resistance of the layer in Ω per square, L is the length along the current in μm, and W is the width in μm. The ratio L/W is the number of squares.

blocks.text: Because a minimum-width wire is the narrowest allowed, it is also the most resistive per unit length. Making a wire wider reduces R in proportion to W.

examples.question: A process uses λ = 0.5 μm with these rules: metal 1 minimum width 3λ, metal 1 minimum spacing 3λ, poly minimum width 2λ, contact 2λ × 2λ, and metal enclosure of a contact 1λ on every side. (a) Find the minimum metal width and the minimum metal pitch in μm. (b) Find the minimum poly width in μm. (c) A transistor is drawn with W = 8λ and L = 2λ. Find its gate area and its gate capacitance, given C_ox = 2.3 fF/μm².
steps: Convert the unit: λ = 0.5 μm, so one λ is 0.5 μm.
Pitch = width + spacing = 3λ + 3λ = 6λ = 6 × 0.5 μm = 3.0 μm, measured centre to centre.
(c) Channel width W = 8λ = 8 × 0.5 μm = 4 μm. Channel length L = 2λ = 2 × 0.5 μm = 1 μm.
Gate area = W × L = 4 μm × 1 μm = 4 μm².
Gate capacitance = C_ox × area = 2.3 fF/μm² × 4 μm² = 9.2 fF.
Check on the enclosure rule: the metal around a 2λ contact must be 4λ × 4λ, that is 2.0 μm × 2.0 μm.
examples.answer: Minimum metal width 1.5 μm, metal pitch 3.0 μm, minimum poly width 1.0 μm, gate area 4 μm² and gate capacitance 9.2 fF.
examples.check:
lam = 0.5
mw = 3*lam
pitch = 6*lam
pw = 2*lam
W = 8*lam
L = 2*lam
area = W*L
C = area*2.3
print(mw)
print(pitch)
print(pw)
print(area)
print(C)

traps: Using λ for both the layout unit and the lithography wavelength. In a layout question λ is the unit; the printer wavelength is a separate number in nm.
Confusing minimum width with minimum spacing. Width is one shape; spacing is the gap between two shapes.
Swapping enclosure and extension. Enclosure surrounds a shape on all sides; extension runs past an edge on one side only.
Computing pitch as width plus twice the spacing, or as width alone. Pitch is one width plus one spacing.
Mixing units halfway: a length in λ multiplied by λ in nm instead of μm, giving an answer off by 1000.

quiz.q: What is λ in a layout rule set?
quiz.a: A single length unit chosen by the foundry, usually half the smallest drawn feature, so that every rule is a whole multiple of it.

quiz.q: Name four rule families found in any design rule set.
quiz.a: Minimum width, minimum spacing, minimum overlap, and enclosure (also extension and separation between unrelated layers).

quiz.q: Why does a rule set need a minimum spacing between two shapes on the same layer?
quiz.a: The gap can close because each of the two shapes may print wider than drawn, from resist and etch bias or lithographic variation. If each edge can move outward by δ, the gap loses 2δ, so minimum spacing keeps a margin larger than that worst-case closing. Misalignment is handled by overlap and enclosure rules between different layers.

quiz.q: A process has λ = 0.25 μm, metal width 4λ and metal spacing 3λ. Find the metal width and the metal pitch in μm.
A contact is 2λ × 2λ and needs a metal enclosure of 1λ on every side. Give the metal square in λ and in μm for λ = 0.4 μm.
quiz.a: Each side grows by 1λ twice: 2λ + 2λ = 4λ. At λ = 0.4 μm this is 1.6 μm, so the metal square is 1.6 μm × 1.6 μm.

quiz.q: A designer draws a metal 1 wire at 2λ where the rule is 3λ. What failure does this risk, and which check catches it?
quiz.a: The wire may break or neck down during etch, because the printed width falls below what the process can resolve reliably. The design rule checker flags the shape as a minimum-width violation before fabrication.

quiz.q: A metal wire has 20 squares on a layer with sheet resistance 0.08 Ω per square. Find its resistance, and say what happens to it if the width is doubled at the same length.
quiz.a: R = R_s × L/W = 0.08 × 20 = 1.6 Ω. Doubling the width halves the number of squares, so R becomes 0.8 Ω.

beyond: Not for the exam. At advanced nodes the rule manual is no longer a set of independent numbers: layouts are forced onto a fixed grid, and many shape combinations are simply forbidden, a style called restricted design rules. Below about 20 nm, one pattern is printed by two or more masks in turn, so the rules must also keep neighbouring shapes compatible with that splitting. Modern practice splits the work between a DRC deck, which is a program in a dedicated language, and a fill step that adds dummy shapes to keep etching uniform. Search for design rule manual, GDSII, DRC deck and layout-versus-schematic if you want to see the industrial form of this chapter.
